title: Strat Chat — Chunking
author: Mutually Assured Instruction Source: mutallyassuredinstruction.substack.com
summary: A practical case for chunking — breaking instruction into small, cognitively manageable pieces — as foundational to effective teaching. Human working memory can hold only 3–7 novel items before becoming overwhelmed, which means teachers who present too much content at once virtually guarantee that students will retain nothing. Chunking is not merely dividing content into segments; it requires understanding the 'exploded diagram' of a concept and sequencing components so each builds on the last. The author walks through a concrete example from VCE Business Management (inputs, processes, outputs) showing how a single standard expands into approximately 15 teachable sub-steps within a 60-minute lesson. Crucially, chunking is only half the battle — checking for understanding within each chunk is what converts sequenced exposure into retained learning. Since so much of teaching is sequential, each piece building on the prior one, failing to chunk properly means building without a foundation: the structure looks fine until assessment pressure exposes what was never actually learned.
points: Human working memory holds 3–7 novel items before becoming overwhelmed; instruction must be deliberately chunked to avoid exceeding this capacity and losing learning entirely.
Chunking is inherently sequential — each piece must build on prior knowledge; teaching without this foundation creates apparent learning that collapses under assessment.
Checking for understanding within each chunk is what distinguishes chunking that produces durable learning from chunking that merely sequences exposure.
New teachers struggle to chunk effectively because expertise is required to see all the small parts that compose a larger concept — novices can't decompose what they can't yet fully see.

Even a 'simple' single-standard lesson point should decompose into ~15 sub-steps with multiple response opportunities per step; a 60-minute class at face value gives students only ~8 chances to respond, far fewer than optimal.
quotes: The human brain is severely limited. Working memory of an average person can range between 3 and 7 novel items as stimuli before it becomes overwhelmed and cannot process any additional information.
We remember what we think about, but we can only think about the things we hold in our working memory.

So much of the work that we do in teaching is sequential in nature. That is, each item that we learn builds on the item prior to it and therefore if we do not break information down into these small palatable chunks then we are building a house without laying the foundation.
Pro tip — keep it simple. Kids switch off if you talk too long. — Bandit Heeler, Show and Tell (2025)
